content: 1. Specimens for chlamydia testing should be collected no sooner than two hours after the patient has last voided. 2. When collecting specimens for chlamydia testing, ensure that specimens for gram-stain smear or Neisseria gonorrhoeae culture are obtained first. 3. For non-culture chlamydia tests, use the swab provided or specified by the manufacturer. 4. Insert the urogenital swab gently into the urethra, to a depth of 1–2 cm in females and 2–4 cm in males. Rotate the swab in one direction for at least one full revolution over a duration of five seconds. 5. After withdrawing the swab, place it in the appropriate transport medium (e.g., for culture, enzyme immunoassay [EIA], or DNA probe testing) or use it to prepare a slide for direct fluorescent antibody (DFA) testing. Quality Assurance of Specimen Collection 6. Without proper quality assurance, more than 10% of specimens may be unsatisfactory due to the presence of secretions or exudate without adequate urethral or endocervical columnar cells. 7. Periodic cytologic evaluation of specimen quality is recommended when using non-DFA tests to ensure proper specimen collection is maintained. Cell Culture for Chlamydia trachomatis 8. A major advantage of cell culture isolation for Chlamydia trachomatis is its specificity, which approaches 100%. 9. In cell culture, organisms from all three chlamydia species (C. trachomatis, C. pneumoniae, and C. psittaci) grow and produce characteristic intracytoplasmic inclusions. 10. The direct visualization of these inclusions contributes to the high specificity of cell culture in identifying chlamydia. 11. The preferred method for identifying inclusions is staining infected cells with a species-specific, monoclonal fluorescein-labeled antibody (FA) for C. trachomatis. 12. Antibodies that bind to chlamydia lipopolysaccharide (LPS) are not specific for C. trachomatis and will also stain inclusions of C. psittaci and C. pneumoniae. 13. The use of C. trachomatis-specific anti-major outer membrane protein (MOMP) antibodies is the presumed method for detecting C. trachomatis in cell culture. 14. The sensitivity of culture ranges from 70% to 90% in experienced laboratories. 15. Cell culture allows for the preservation of the organism for additional studies, such as determining immunotype (serovar) and antimicrobial susceptibilities. Limitations of Cell Culture 16. Cell culture is technically challenging and requires 3–7 days to yield results. 17. Only viable organisms are detected, necessitating the use of special transport media and strict adherence to transportation and storage temperature requirements. 18. Some specimens may contain contaminating microorganisms or substances toxic to the cell monolayers used for isolating chlamydia. Indications for the Use of Cell Culture 19. A high-quality culture system is the diagnostic method of choice for chlamydia in all medical or legal situations. 20. Culture serves as the standard for quality assurance of non-culture tests and for evaluating new diagnostic methods. 21. Culture is recommended for specimens where non-culture methods are unavailable, inadequately evaluated, or perform poorly. 22. Culture is specifically recommended for specimens from the following sites: Urethral specimens (women and asymptomatic men). Nasopharyngeal specimens (infants). Rectal specimens (all patients, regardless of age). Vaginal specimens (prepubertal girls). Collecting Specimens for Cell Culture 23. Swabs with plastic or wire shafts can be used to collect specimens for cell culture. 24. Swab tips may be made of cotton, rayon, Dacron, or calcium alginate. 25. Swabs with wooden shafts should not be used, as wood may contain substances toxic to chlamydia. 26. Routine quality control should include screening each lot of swabs for potential toxicity to chlamydia. 27. Substituting an endocervical brush for a swab may increase the sensitivity of culture for endocervical specimens in nonpregnant women, though it may induce bleeding. 28. Patients should be informed about the possibility of spotting if an endocervical brush is used. Transporting Cell Culture Specimens 29. The viability of chlamydia organisms must be maintained during transport to the laboratory. 30. Consult the laboratory regarding the selection of appropriate transport medium and procedures. 31. Specimens for culture should be stored at 4°C and inoculated into cell culture as quickly as possible, ideally within 24 hours. 32. If inoculation cannot occur within 24 hours, specimens should be stored at -70°C or colder. 33. Specimens should never be stored at -20°C or in frost-free freezers, as these conditions reduce chlamydia viability. 34. Only cell lines verified for their ability to support chlamydial growth should be used. Analyzing Cell Culture Specimens 35. The identification of C. trachomatis should be based on visualizing characteristic chlamydia inclusions using species-specific FA staining. 36. Laboratories should periodically assess whether multiple passages increase sensitivity. Notes on Specificity 37. The specificity of culture is based on the identification of characteristic inclusions. 38. Identification of chlamydia after culture using EIA or other methods that do not identify characteristic intracytoplasmic inclusions is not recommended. Interpreting Cell Culture Results 39. A positive cell culture and visualization of characteristic inclusions using species-specific monoclonal FA staining are required to diagnose a chlamydial infection. 40. With proper technique, the specificity of cell culture isolation for C. trachomatis is nearly 100%. 41. A negative chlamydia culture does not rule out the presence of a chlamydial infection. 42. The sensitivity of culture is approximately 70%–90% when recommended laboratory and specimen collection techniques are followed. Quality Assurance of Cell Culture Specimen Collection 43. The isolation and detection of chlamydia in cell culture are technically demanding processes.
